title: Cantiague
summary: Cantiague preserves Tooker's Cantiaque, Cantiagge, and Kiscasutta boundary-tree names for marked points of trees on the Hempstead and Oyster Bay plains. The modern marker is approximate, using the Cantiague Park area in Hicksville as a general location basis.
map_geometry_source: Approximate modern Cantiague Park point; original Cantiaque was a boundary point of trees and not an exact park coordinate.
why_this_matters: Cantiague preserves boundary-tree language from the Hempstead and Oyster Bay plains, with meanings tied to marked, chopped, or blazed trees. That detail matters because trees could function as public memory, navigation, and boundary markers in Native and colonial land records. Even suburban Nassau County landscapes carry older Indigenous systems of orientation and land relationship.
introduction_content: Cantiaque, also written Cantiagge, is recorded as a point of trees on the bounds between Hempstead and Oyster Bay. The modern name Cantiague survives in the Hicksville area, but the original boundary mark was more specific than today's park location.
translation_content:
Recorded forms include Cantiaque, Cantiagge, Cantiag, and Kiscasutta. The name is interpreted these boundary-tree names through words for marking, chopping, or blazing trees. For Kiscasutta, he gives the sense as marked trees, chopped trees, or trees blazed for a boundary mark.

Why Place Names Matter

“Indigenous placenames reflect Aboriginal views on life and are an integral part of their storytelling.”

— Luise Hercus, Indigenous toponymy: Part 1 (2018), Placenames Australia, p. 1, point 11
whereintheworld_content: The map placement is a general Cantiague Park / Hicksville-area point used to orient the boundary-tree placename cluster, not the exact 1653, 1666, 1677, or 1685 tree location, and the Kiscasutta point northeast of Hempstead needs further map review.
